title: Agents
text: Agents Crafting An agent is a frame that runs a program. Walking, carrying, reaping, mining and laying blocks are its own; where learning beats a rule, a model in one of its slots decides, in exactly the format of that model's test, and the agent does what the model answers. You can see a model in its lantern of a head, turning faster while it thinks. Home and models Where you place an agent is its home, and its work happens around home. Set home makes where it stands its new home. It has two model slots. Its Model takes a Checkpoint with a model of up to 40,000 parameters, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, for a model of any size: see Serving Models. This model writes the orders you give as programs, and makes the decisions of farming, storing, hauling and building. Its Filter takes a checkpoint that passes Sorting, and tells what kind each thing is. Its screen says what is missing. Programs The Program tab holds what it does when nothing else is asked of it: steps between commas, checked as you type. take bread, come, give bread repeat (harvest, plant wheat seeds, put wheat) if ripe (harvest) else (wait 10) until full (pickup) Run starts it and Stop stops it. A program that goes on for good, a repeat without a count, is its standing work; any other runs once, and then it rests. The buttons on the Work tab set ready-made programs: Farm is repeat (farm), Sort is repeat (sort), and so on, and Rest clears it. The + beside Stop lays out every piece of a program to click together instead of typing, each saying what it does when you point at it. Pieces go on the end, along with whatever plainly comes next: the ( that opens a block, the mark a place needs. To name a thing, pick it up and click the program, or the order box. The steps: come, home, go 3 to the third mark, stay, follow take 5 bread from the chests and barrels around home, put everything or put wheat away, give bread to you, fetch bread, which is taking, coming and giving pickup what lies around it, harvest, plant wheat seeds, till the grass near water, mine 4 stone (with a pickaxe it carries, for blocks that need one), place oak planks 2 on top of the second mark wait 10 seconds, say hello farm, store, sort, haul or build: one round of a routine Blocks: repeat (…), repeat 3 (…), if … (…) else (…), until … (…) and wait until …. Checks: have 3 bread, stocked bread in the stores around home, ripe, full, night, near (you are within 8 blocks), powered 2 (the second mark has a redstone signal), each with not before it if need be. The trace The Trace tab shows what it did, checked and decided, newest last, and how each step went: storing and sorting note every stack they put away, and where. A step that fails says why, and the program goes on with the next. An agent that gets stuck on its way somewhere gives up after a while; stuck three times running, it jumps home. Routines farm: walks the farmland within 7 blocks of home. At each plot it shows its model the plots it has seen so far and asks what to do with this one. It harvests, waits or plants as told, and takes the harvest to the chest at home, keeping some seed. store: empties the barrels around home into the chests within 8 blocks, numbered 0 to 9, nearest first. A kind it has never seen goes to the emptiest chest. For a kind seen before, it shows its model where eight kinds went and asks which chest this one belongs in. sort: empties the barrels around home into the chests labelled with each thing's kind: Food, Plants, Wood, Stone, Ores or Tools. Name a chest in an anvil to label it, or fix a sign to it. Its filter is asked the kind of each thing by its name alone, so it can sort things it has never seen. Whatever its filter calls other, or is less than 60% sure of, goes in a chest labelled Other, or else in one with no label. haul: walks out along the six waymarks it was handed, loads up from the chest or barrel at the last one, and comes home. On the way back its model names the waymarks in reverse, and it walks wherever its model says. build: carries on a straight row on top of the blocks between two marks, laying blocks from the chests at home. It shows its model the row so far, a letter for each kind of block, and lays whatever its model says comes next. Lay the first round of the pattern yourself, starting above the first mark. The Survey Rod Crafting Use a Survey Rod on blocks to mark them, up to eight, in order; use a marked block again to unmark it, and sneak-use in the air to clear them all. Use the rod on an agent to hand it the marks: waymarks for hauling, the blocks under the two ends of a row for building, or places for go and place. Program Cards Crafting (Shapeless) A Program Card carries a program from agent to agent. Use a blank card on an agent to copy its program, and a written one to hand the program over; sneak-use a written card to copy onto it instead. In an agent's screen, click the program holding a written card to load what it says, or holding a blank card to write the program onto it; shift-click writes onto a written card too. Orders Start a chat message with an agent's name to give it an order: Pip, bring me some bread. It hears you within 24 blocks, or anywhere a Model Server's relays reach while you are in reach too, holding a Terminal tuned to it. You can also type an order in its screen. Its model writes the order as a program. One step, or one of the jobs, it does at once. Anything else it reads back with [Do it] and [Cancel] to click in chat, or on the Work tab of its screen, and runs only once you say yes. An order comes before its program, which it goes back to after. If what its model writes is no program at all, it is puzzled; a model that never practised orders will mostly be puzzled.

title: The Archive
text: The Archive The old world wrote letters, journals, stories, songs, recipes, manuals and notices, and kept a copy of everything. What survives is in Archive Shards, each a piece of one record with some of its text lost. Shards A shard learns which record it is the first time you hold it. Use it to read what is left; lost text shows as ▒. Archive drives Crafting Use an Archive Drive to file every shard you carry into it. Shards of the same record make one better copy: whatever any of them kept is kept. The drive's tooltip counts its records and its legible letters. In a Model Core's Data slots, a drive is practice for Reading: the model learns to predict the next letter of everything legible on it, or the next token with a tokenizer, so the more you recover, the more it has to learn from. Reading is tested on records no shard ever carries. A model can only pass by learning how the old world wrote, not by remembering what it read. The Reader Crafting A Reader restores lost text. Put a shard in its tray and a model in its model slot: a checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server for a model too big to hold. The Reader goes through the lost blocks one by one. For each, the model reads the text just before the block and then guesses the block letter by letter, seeing each true letter after its guess. If it guesses at least half of them, the block was predictable enough to restore, and it comes back. A block the model cannot restore stays lost until a better model tries. A model that reads ahead, seeing the letter it is asked to guess, is turned away: it would only copy.

title: The Bench and the Fabricator
text: The Bench and the Fabricator Every machine is made in a Fabricator. The simple ones need nothing but materials. The rest need a Blank Photomask carrying a design for what they compute, and designs are wired on a Bench from the smallest operations there are. Crafting Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Crafting (Shapeless) Specs The Bench lists specs: what a module must compute, a formula, and a set of test cases with the answers worked out exactly. Some cases are ordinary. Others are the inputs that break the obvious design: scores of a thousand, a row of equal numbers, numbers far from zero. A design passes when it gets every case right to within a thousandth. Specs build on each other. Attention needs your softmax and matrix multiply; the transformer block needs layer norm, attention and the feed-forward block. A spec opens when the ones it builds on are verified. Wiring a design Drag parts from the left onto the board, and drag from one node's right edge to another's left edge to wire them. Every node shows a strip of the numbers it computes on the chosen case; click it to read them. A strip turning red means a value that is not a number, and the node that turned it red is the one to look at. Wire your last node into result, and the cases on the right tell you which pass and why the others don't. The parts: Sources: a constant you type, and size, the length of the last axis. Arithmetic: add, sub, mul, div and max, element by element. An axis of size 1 stretches to match the other input, so a row of sums divides a whole row of numbers. Functions: neg, exp, log, sqrt and tanh. Last axis: sum and amax keep the axis with size 1; transpose swaps the last two axes; unsqueeze and squeeze add and drop an axis of size 1; causal hides everything above the diagonal. Your modules: every spec you have verified, as one part. Recording When every case passes, Record to photomask writes the design onto a blank photomask from your inventory, signed with your name. The spec counts as verified for you from then on, and its module joins your parts on every Bench. Fabricating Put a photomask in the Fabricator and pick a machine. Each takes a Tensor Casing, wafers, and weight crystals if it learns weights. A design's area sets the wafers: four units of area to a wafer. Each primitive costs a little area and each module what its spec's design costs, so a smaller design makes cheaper machines. The photomask is never used up. Without a mask, the Fabricator makes the machines that need no design: the embedding and position tables, the residual junction, the gate, the scaler, the causal mask, the head splitter and merger, the delay line and the concatenator. A matrix multiply photomask also makes the Training Accelerator. Fused and unfused The ruins hold old photomasks too, carrying salvaged designs: correct, but written out one primitive at a time. Machines made from them are unfused. They give the same answers, but they write out every tensor in between, so they use more memory and train more slowly. A design you verify yourself makes fused machines, one kernel each. The machine's screen and tooltip say which it is.

title: The Model Core
text: The Model Core The Model Core feeds text into your machines and judges what comes back. Its front sends out tokens; every other face takes in the model's scores. It trains the model, tests it, and saves it as a model. The trained weights stay in the machines themselves, so a model keeps what it learned when you leave and come back. Crafting Data Four slots for what the model practises on: datasets, archive drives, or a salvaged model. Everything in them is practised together, a batch from each in turn. Beside them are the tokenizer slot, for the tokens the model reads and writes, and the checkpoint slot, with what the checkpoint in it holds. Save to checkpoint tests the model on every benchmark and saves it into that checkpoint. With a salvaged model loaded, Rebuild builds its machines in front of the Core: see Salvaged Models. Train The learning curve, the current numbers and the training settings. See Training for what each one means. Params counts the model's weights; Grad norm is the size of the last gradient; Threads is how many threads the Core trains with. Tests Every benchmark, its score at the last test, and the score that passes. The test of each benchmark is taken while the model trains on it; Test all runs every test now. Hover over an benchmark for the format its test uses. See Models and Tests. Try Runs the model. Choose an benchmark: Example draws a fresh test example and shows the model answering it, the way an agent would ask. For Orders, type an order and Ask; for Reading, type the start of something and Write: the model carries it on one letter at a time, drawing each from its predicted probabilities. Temp (temperature) sharpens or flattens those probabilities before drawing: Low temperatures repeat the model's favourite continuations; high ones take more risks. The bars show how likely the model found each candidate for the first letter it wrote. Inspect Every machine of the model in the order data reaches it, with its output shape, its number of weights and the size of its last gradient. Problems found by Check are listed here too. A bar that shrinks to nothing as you go down the list is a gradient that never arrives. More threads Each Training Accelerator touching the Core, directly or through other Accelerators, lends it one more thread, up to the limit the server allows. An Accelerator with nothing to cool it runs hot and lends half: give it water, ice or snow to touch. The Fabricator makes them from a matrix multiply photomask.

title: Serving Models
text: Serving Models A model too big for an agent's head can still work for it. A Model Server holds the model and answers questions for everything tuned to it, as far as its relays reach. The Model Server Crafting (Shapeless) Use a saved Checkpoint on a Model Server to load its model; sneak-use the server with an empty hand to take the checkpoint back. Use it to see what it is doing: the model it serves, how many answers a second it can give, how many questions are waiting and how many it has answered. A server gives 4 answers a second on its own. Each Training Accelerator touching it adds as many again, or half as many while it runs hot. Its front lights blink while it answers. When more than 64 questions wait, new ones are turned away until it catches up. Relays Crafting (Shapeless) A Model Server reaches 16 blocks by itself. A Relay within 32 blocks of the server, or of another relay already linked to it, links up and carries the server's reach 32 blocks around itself. Use a relay to see how many other relays are in reach and which servers it is linked to. Relay Cards Crafting (Shapeless) Use a Relay Card on a Model Server to tune it. In an agent's or a Reader's model slot, the card asks the server instead of carrying a model: any size of model, wherever the server's network reaches. Every agent tuned to one server shares its answers per second. The Terminal Crafting (Shapeless) Tune a Terminal on a Model Server the same way, then use it to talk to the served model: write the start of something and the model carries it on. While you hold a tuned Terminal within the server's reach, every agent the server reaches hears the orders you give by name in chat. Heat Accelerators run hot. One touching water, ice or snow, or standing in a cold biome, lends a full thread to a Core or a full share of answers to a server; one with nothing to cool it lends half, and smokes while it works.

title: The Forecaster
text: The Forecaster The Forecaster watches the crops around it and writes down what they do. Give it a model that has learned how crops grow, and if the model's forecasts match the field, it runs the field ahead: it draws each crop's next looks from the model and makes them so. Crafting Watching Every twenty seconds the Forecaster looks at every crop within four blocks of it, on its own level and one above or below: wheat, carrots, potatoes, and any crop that grows through the same seven ages. Each crop gets a line: its age at every look, from 0 when planted to 7 when ripe, ending once it has been seen ripe twice. 00000011111111122222223333333334444445555555666666677 Only growth a crop made by itself counts. A crop that is harvested, trampled or fed bone meal starts a new line, so its lines only ever hold what the field really does. Put a Field Log in the Log slot to keep a copy. Crafting (Shapeless) A model of a field A model that has learned what happens next is a model of its world, and the Forecaster asks for nothing more. Train one on Forecasting at a Model Core: the Growth Dataset holds the lines of many fields. Crafting (Shapeless) How fast a crop grows depends on its field: wet farmland or dry, in tidy rows or crowded. A model that learned from many fields expects the growth of an average one. That is close enough on some fields and far off on others. To forecast your own field, train on it. Put the Forecaster's Field Log in a data slot of the Core, on its own, and the model learns this field's pace. It gets worse at fields in general, and may even fail the Forecasting test: that is the price of fitting one field well. Beside the Growth Dataset, the log only pulls the model halfway. Calibration A forecast is only worth acting on if it is right on average. Before it runs anything, once its crops have grown 100 ages by themselves, the Forecaster checks the model against everything it watched, lines still being written included: the crops that finish first are the ones that happened to grow fastest, so finished lines alone would flatter a model that expects too much. At every look it adds up the growth the model expected, and divides by the growth there was: Within 11% of 1, it runs the field four looks for every one. Within 25%, two. Further off, it refuses the model. The screen shows the field from above, then the growth per look from each age: amber for what the field did, teal for what the model expected. A model that expects too much from young crops, or too little from old ones, shows it there. A refused model is checked again each time the field grows 25 more ages, and any model is checked again when it changes. Running ahead At every look, each growing crop's line goes to the model, which draws the crop's next look from its probabilities, then the next, as many as the model has earned. The crop grows to the age drawn. Lines the model wrote are never written down: its log only ever holds what the field did by itself.

title: Getting Started
text: Getting Started A first model fits in a few blocks: a Model Core, an Embedding Table and some Signal Cable. It will learn to farm. Then you give it a body. Materials Tensor Casing is the shell of every machine; Weight Crystal holds learned numbers, so machines with weights need them. Crafting Crafting Then craft the Model Core, a stack of cables and a Field Dataset: endless practice at farming. Crafting Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Machines are made in a Fabricator. With no photomask in it, it makes the Embedding Table from a casing, a Wafer and a weight crystal. Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Build it Place the Model Core. Its front turns toward you: tokens come out of it. Lay a cable from the Core's front to a free spot a few blocks away. Place the Embedding Table against the end of that cable. It snaps into the flow: its back reads the cable and its front points away. Lay a cable from the table's front back to any other face of the Core: its sides, its top or its back. That is where the model's scores go in. Open the table and set Width to V (vocab). The two cables never touch, so they form two separate networks: one carries tokens to the table, the other carries the table's scores back. Train it Open the Core and put the Field Dataset in one of its Data slots. Switch to Train and press Train. Two curves fall: the loss on practice, and the loss on the test, which only uses plots the model never practised on. Farming takes little thought: harvest a ripe plot, plant a bare one, leave anything else to grow. An Embedding Table set to V scores the next character from the one before it, and the character before each decision is the plot, so this one table can learn all of farming. When Reacting on the Tests tab passes 98%, the model is ready. Save it Craft a Checkpoint, put it in the Core's checkpoint slot and press Save to checkpoint. The Core tests the model on every benchmark and keeps it, scores and all, in the crystal. The machines can go on training; the checkpoint keeps this moment. Crafting Give it a body Craft an Agent and place it beside some farmland with a chest nearby: where it stands becomes its home. Open it, put the checkpoint in its Model slot, hand it a few seeds and choose Farm. Crafting It walks the farmland around home. At every plot it asks its model what to do, in exactly the format of the test, and does what the model answers. Its screen shows what it asked and what came back. Walking, reaping and carrying are the body's work; every decision is your model's. Further Other datasets teach other jobs, and better models need machines built from designs: wire them yourself on a Bench, or go looking for the old ones in the ruins. Look at any machine to see its name, its output shape (or what is wrong with it) and what the face you are looking at does. Sneak-use a machine's face to point its output there. Training runs on its own threads. Place Training Accelerator blocks against the Core to give it more, and keep them cool.

title: Residual
text: Residual Someone lived here before you. They built machines that thought, and they wrote everything down. Then they were gone. Pieces of what they left still turn up in the ruins: broken tablets of their writing, the designs of their machines, and models that no longer work. These are field notes on building models again: language models made of machines that each do one operation, cabled into a network, trained on text, and tested on text they have never seen. A good one can farm, keep a storeroom, run errands, carry on a pattern, tell what a thing is by its name, understand what you tell it, read what the old world wrote, and see where a field is going. Start here Getting Started: a first model, and a body for it. Ruins: where the old world's things are. The Archive: shards, drives, and restoring what was lost. Milestones: every advancement, lit once you have made it, and how to make the rest. Models The Bench and the Fabricator: designs wired from primitives, and the machines made from them. The Model Core: where models are built, trained, tested and saved. Tokens: the BPE Forge, and vocabularies learned from the archive. Training: reading a loss curve, and the settings that shape it. Models and Tests: the eight benchmarks, checkpoints, and how big a model may be. Salvaged Models: broken models from the ruins. Putting models to work Agents: frames that run programs, with models where learning beats a rule. The Forecaster: a model of a field, trusted only as far as it is right. Serving Models: Model Servers, relays and the Terminal. Reference Machines and Cables: how values travel between blocks. The Residual Stream: the running sum every transformer layer reads and adds to. Shapes: what [B×T×C] means, and how to fix a shape error. Machines, one page each.

title: Activation
text: Activation Bends every number through the same nonlinear function. Without one, two Linear Layers in a row multiply out into a single Linear Layer, however many you stack: the activation is what lets depth add anything. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Settings Function: ReLU by default. ReLU keeps positive numbers and zeroes the rest. Its slope is 0 or 1, so it never shrinks a gradient that passes. GELU is a smooth ReLU, used by GPT-2 and BERT. SiLU is z·σ(z), used inside the feed-forward layers of LLaMA and its relatives. tanh squashes into (−1, 1), as in the first neural language models. sigmoid squashes into (0, 1). Its slope is at most a quarter, so every sigmoid layer shrinks the gradient that passes back through it. Parameters None. In PyTorch F.relu(x) F.gelu(x, approximate="tanh") F.silu(x) torch.tanh(x) torch.sigmoid(x) Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of GELU: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Residual Junction
text: Residual Junction Adds its two inputs, number by number. It has two jobs. It combines token and position vectors, and it makes residual connections: adding a branch's output back onto the stream that went into it, so the branch refines the stream instead of replacing it. Shapes Two equal shapes, or a smaller one that matches the end of the larger and repeats across it: [B×T×C] and [T×C] make [B×T×C]. Parameters None. In PyTorch x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) Notes The identity term in its gradient gives every layer a direct path back to the loss. That is why stacks of residual layers keep learning when plain stacks stall. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Attention Head
text: Attention Head Multi-head causal self-attention in one machine: the attention you can build from Linear Layers, a Matrix Multiplier, a Causal Mask and a Softmax, with queries, keys and values all computed from its one input, a causal mask built in, several heads and an output projection. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. The width C must divide evenly by it. Each head works on C/H of the numbers and scales its scores by 1/√(C/H). Parameters 4 × C²: the matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O, without biases. In PyTorch self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(C, heads=4) x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) Notes After training, its picture shows where its first head looks: one row per position, one column for every position it can see. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Attention: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Causal Mask
text: Causal Mask Sets every score above the diagonal of a T × T grid to −∞. After a Softmax those become weights of exactly zero, so position t gives no weight to anything after t. Shapes A grid of scores […×T×T] in, the same shape out. Parameters None. In PyTorch def causal_mask(scores): T = scores.shape[-1] future = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1) return scores.masked_fill(future, float("-inf")) Notes It belongs between the scores and the Softmax. Without it, a model trained to predict the next token can simply read it, and its loss falls to almost nothing while it learns nothing. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Concatenator
text: Concatenator Joins two vectors end to end: the main input's numbers first, then the side input's. Shapes […×a] and […×b] in, […×(a + b)] out. Every size but the last must match. Parameters None. In PyTorch x = torch.cat([a, b], dim=-1) Notes A Linear Layer after a Concatenator computes the same thing as two Linear Layers, one on each input, added together. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Embedding Table
text: Embedding Table Looks up a learned row of numbers for each token: token i gets row i of a table with one row per vocabulary entry. This is how text enters a model, so the table must be fed directly by the Model Core's front. Shapes Tokens [B×T] in, [B×T×C] out, where C is the Width. Settings Width: V, or 4 to 256. 32 by default. At V, each row can serve directly as the scores for the next token: a bigram model. Parameters V × C, drawn from a normal distribution with spread 1. In PyTorch self.embed = nn.Embedding(V, C) e = self.embed(tokens) Notes After training, the weights picture shows the table, a row per token. Tokens that behave alike end up with similar rows, which is how what the model learns about one carries over to others. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Machines
text: Machines Each machine performs one operation of a model, with the same arithmetic as PyTorch. A machine takes its main input on its back and, if it has one, its side input on any other face, and sends its result out of its front: see Machines and Cables. Right-click a machine to change its settings and see what it computes. Every machine comes out of the Fabricator. The simple ones need no design; the rest need a photomask of the spec that describes them, verified on a Bench or salvaged from the ruins. No design needed Embedding Table: token ids to vectors. Position Table: a learned vector for every position. Residual Junction: addition, and with it the residual stream. Gate: one signal opening or closing another. Scaler: multiplied by a constant, usually 1/√d. Causal Mask: the future hidden. Head Splitter and Head Merger: multi-head attention from parts. Delay Line: a fixed look back in time. Concatenator: two vectors joined end to end. From a design Matrix Multiplier, from Matrix Multiply: grids multiplied, keys compared with queries. Softmax, from Softmax: scores turned into weights. Linear Layer, from Linear Layer: a learned matrix, the workhorse of every model. Activation, from GELU: a nonlinear function on every number. Normalizer, from Layer Norm: vectors kept at a steady size. Attention Head, from Attention: multi-head attention in one machine. Feed-Forward Block, from Feed-Forward Block: widen, bend, project back. Transformer Block, from Transformer Block: a whole transformer layer.

title: Linear Layer
text: Linear Layer Multiplies every vector by a learned matrix and adds a learned bias. It works on the last size only: every position of every sequence goes through the same weights, separately. Shapes […×C_in] in, […×C_out] out, where C_out is the Outputs setting. Settings Outputs: V, or 4 to 256. 32 by default. End a model with a Linear Layer whose Outputs is V: those are the scores the Core wants. Bias: on by default. Parameters C_in × C_out, plus C_out for the bias. They start as PyTorch's do: uniform within ±1/√C_in, with the bias at zero. In PyTorch self.hidden = nn.Linear(C_in, C_out) h = self.hidden(x) Notes PyTorch stores the matrix the other way round, as [C_out × C_in]. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Linear Layer: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Matrix Multiplier
text: Matrix Multiplier Multiplies two grids of numbers, the main input on the left and the side input on the right. In attention it does two jobs: comparing every query with every key, with Transpose on, and mixing the values by the weights that come out of the softmax. Shapes […×n×k] and […×k×m] in, […×n×m] out. With Transpose on, the side input is […×m×k]. The sizes in front must match, or the side input can be a single [k×m] grid shared by all. Settings Transpose: off by default. Flips the side input's last two sizes before multiplying. Parameters None: both inputs come from other machines. In PyTorch scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) mixed = weights @ v Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Matrix Multiply: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Head Merger
text: Head Merger Joins the heads back into one vector per position: the reverse of the Head Splitter. Shapes [B×H×T×d] in, [B×T×(H·d)] out. Parameters None. In PyTorch def merge_heads(x): B, H, T, D = x.shape return x.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, H * D) Notes Follow it with a Linear Layer to mix what the heads found: that is the output projection, W_O. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Feed-Forward Block
text: Feed-Forward Block Two Linear Layers with an Activation between them: widen each vector, bend it, project it back. It works on every position separately. Attention moves information between positions; this block processes it in place. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Expand: 1, 2 or 4. 4 by default. The hidden width is Expand × C. Function: ReLU, GELU or SiLU. GELU by default. Parameters 2 × E × C² + E × C + C, where E is Expand. In PyTorch self.ffn = FeedForward(C, 4 * C, gelu_tanh) x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x)) Notes With Expand at 4, it holds two thirds of a transformer layer's weights. Interpretability research suggests these layers store much of what a model knows about the world. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Feed-Forward Block: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Gate
text: Gate Multiplies its two inputs number by number, so one signal can scale, open or close another. Shapes The same shapes as the Residual Junction takes. Parameters None. In PyTorch y = F.silu(self.gate(x)) * self.up(x) Notes Gates sit inside the feed-forward layers of most recent language models. SwiGLU multiplies SiLU(xW₁) by a second projection xW₃ before projecting back down. To build one: two Linear Layers reading the same input, an Activation set to SiLU after one of them, a Gate joining them, and a Linear Layer back to the original width. LSTMs, the recurrent networks that came before transformers, controlled their memory with gates like this. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Normalizer
text: Normalizer Rescales each vector to a steady size, then applies a learned gain and, for LayerNorm, a learned offset. Shapes […×C] in, the same shape out. Each vector is normalized over its last size. Settings Kind: LayerNorm by default, or RMSNorm, which skips the mean and the offset. LLaMA uses RMSNorm. Parameters 2 × C for LayerNorm, C for RMSNorm. ε is 1e-5. In PyTorch self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(C) h = self.norm1(x) Notes Put one at the start of each branch, before attention or the feed-forward block, and one before the final Linear Layer. This pre-norm layout is GPT-2's, and nearly every model since uses it. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Layer Norm: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Position Table
text: Position Table A learned vector for every position in the context, from 0 to T − 1. It takes no input. Add its output to the token vectors with a Residual Junction, and every position carries both what it is and where it is. Shapes No input. [T×C] out, which a Residual Junction adds to every sequence in the batch. Settings Width: 4 to 256. 32 by default. Match it to the Embedding Table's width. Parameters T × C, where T is the context length, 64. In PyTorch self.pos = nn.Embedding(T, C) x = self.embed(tokens) + self.pos(torch.arange(T)) Notes Learned positions are what GPT-2 used. Most recent models instead rotate each query and key by an angle that depends on its position (RoPE), so that attention scores depend on how far apart two tokens are. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Scaler
text: Scaler Multiplies everything by a constant. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Settings Factor: 1/√d by default, where d is the last size of the input. Also 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 2 and 4. Parameters None. In PyTorch q = q / math.sqrt(d) Notes In attention it does not matter much where the 1/√d goes: scaling the queries or scaling the scores gives the same result. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Delay Line
text: Delay Line Shifts a sequence later in time: position t receives what position t − k had, and the first k positions receive zeros. It lets a position see a fixed number of steps back. Shapes A sequence […×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Steps: 1 to 4. 1 by default. Parameters None. In PyTorch def delay(x, steps): return F.pad(x, (0, 0, steps, 0))[..., : x.shape[-2], :] prev = delay(e, 1) Notes Attention can look back any distance, so transformers rarely need a fixed delay. Some architectures keep one anyway: RWKV mixes every token with the one before it, a learned blend called token shift. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Softmax
text: Softmax Turns each row of scores into weights that are positive and sum to one, along the last size. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Parameters None. In PyTorch weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) Notes Don't end a model with one. The Core applies its own softmax to the scores it receives, as PyTorch's cross-entropy loss does, and a second one squashes them so flat that the model can never be confident. In an attention build, the Softmax's output picture is the attention pattern: one row per position. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Softmax: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Head Splitter
text: Head Splitter Cuts each vector into H equal parts and gives the heads a dimension of their own, so the machines after it work on every head at once. Shapes [B×T×C] in, [B×H×T×(C/H)] out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. Parameters None. In PyTorch def split_heads(x, heads): B, T, C = x.shape return x.view(B, T, heads, C // heads).transpose(1, 2) Notes With a Head Splitter and a Head Merger you can build multi-head attention from parts: split the queries, keys and values the same way, and the Matrix Multipliers, Scaler, Causal Mask and Softmax all work on every head in parallel. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Transformer Block
text: Transformer Block One whole transformer layer in one machine: normalize, attend, add back; normalize, feed forward, add back. Stack them to make a GPT. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. Expand: 1, 2 or 4. 4 by default. Function: ReLU, GELU or SiLU. GELU by default. Parameters 12 × C² + 9 × C with Expand at 4: about 50,000 at width 64. In PyTorch self.block1 = Block(C, heads=4, hidden=4 * C, act=gelu_tanh) x = self.block1(x) Notes Its picture shows the attention pattern of its first head, like the Attention Head's. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Transformer Block: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Milestones
text: Milestones Every milestone is an advancement, in the frame the advancement screen gives it, and the frame lights up once you have made it. They run roughly in the order a world unfolds, though most chapters can be taken in any order. A first model Checkpoint Save a trained model. Cable an Embedding Table to a Model Core, train it on the Field Dataset and save it: Getting Started. Harvest Time Save a model that passes the Reacting test. Saving tests a model on every benchmark; a first model passes this one once it has practised long enough. Agent Make an agent. Craft one, place it beside some farmland and give it your checkpoint: Agents. Hello, World Give an agent a program of your own. Type one in its screen, or click it together from the palette. The old world Ruins Find a ruin of the people who were here before. Archive houses, relay masts and buried vaults stand far apart: Ruins. Lost Words Dig an archive shard out of a ruin. Each is a piece of one record, with some of its text lost: The Archive. The Archive Make an archive drive to file shards into. Shards of the same record filed together make one better copy. Restoration Place a Reader. It restores a record's lost text with a model of yours. Words, Not Letters Learn a vocabulary in a BPE Forge. A vocabulary learned from what you have recovered lets a model read words instead of letters: Tokens. It Reads Save a model that passes the Reading test. Train on an Archive Drive until the test loss is 1.40 or less: Models and Tests. Machines from scratch The Bench Place a Bench, where modules are wired from primitives. Each spec comes with cases that break the obvious design: The Bench and the Fabricator. Lithography Place a Fabricator, which makes machines from designs. Photomasks found in the ruins work in it too. Rows by Columns Verify a design for Matrix Multiply. The Layer Verify a design for the Linear Layer. It opens once matrix multiply is verified. Feed Forward Verify a design for the Feed-Forward Block. It opens once the linear layer is verified. On Average Verify a design for Mean. In Range Verify a layer norm that survives flat and far rows. It opens once mean is verified. A Smooth Bend Verify a design for GELU. Overflow Verify a softmax that survives large scores. Scores of a thousand overflow the obvious design. Paying Attention Verify a design for Attention. It opens once softmax is verified. The Block Verify a design for the Transformer Block. It opens once attention is verified. From Scratch Verify every spec on the Bench. Residual Lay a residual stream, the backbone every transformer is built around. Transformer layers read from it and add to it: The Residual Stream. Models that work Each benchmark is passed by saving a model that passes it; the table in Models and Tests says what to practise for each. A Place for Everything Save a model that passes the Recall test. Practise on the Storage Dataset. The Way Home Save a model that passes the Reversal test. Practise on the Errand Dataset. Once More From the Top Save a model that passes the Induction test. Practise on the Pattern Dataset; it takes two layers of attention. Pigeonholes Save a model that passes the Sorting test. Practise on the Sorting Dataset. What Comes Next Save a model that passes the Forecasting test. Practise on the Growth Dataset. Plain Words Save a model that passes the Orders test. Practise on the Orders Dataset; it takes a model too big to carry. A Whole Model Save one model that passes every test. A Model Core practises up to four kinds at once. Putting models to work A Watched Field Place a Forecaster by your crops. It writes down how the crops around it grow: The Forecaster. Ahead of Time Have a Forecaster grow your crops with a model it trusts. Train a model on the Forecaster's own log until it trusts it. At Your Service Place a Model Server. A bigger model stays in a server and answers over relays: Serving Models. Within Reach Place a relay. The plans turn up on relay masts and in vaults. Do What I Mean Have an agent carry out an order its model understood. Start a chat message with its name, such as Pip, bring me some bread. Its model has to have practised orders. Salvage Salvage Find a salvaged model in a ruin. Each one failed in its own way: Salvaged Models. Answering Repair the field model that never answered. No Peeking Repair the field model that was never wrong. First and Last Repair the errand model that came home the wrong way. Steady Hands Repair the storeroom model that burned out. Shortcuts Repair the tall model that never learned to read.

title: Models and Tests
text: Models and Tests Every model is tested on eight benchmarks. Each test uses examples practice never shows, and each job asks its model in exactly the test's format, so a test score is how often an agent will decide right. Benchmark Practice The test Passes at Used for Reacting Field Dataset plots, and what to do with each 98% farming Forecasting Growth Dataset crops' ages at every look loss ≤ 0.23 the Forecaster Recall Storage Dataset goods and their chests, then one kind asked again 90% storing Reversal Errand Dataset waymarks on the way out, then the way home 90% hauling Induction Pattern Dataset letters where a run comes round again 90% building Sorting Sorting Dataset things named, and the kind of each, some made up 90% sorting Orders Orders Dataset orders, and what was meant by them 90% orders Reading Archive Drive records no shard carries loss ≤ 1.40 the Reader Hover over a benchmark on the Core's Tests tab for the exact format. The Try tab shows the model answering a fresh example, the way an agent would ask it. Practising several things The Core's four Data slots are practised together: every step draws its batch from one of them in turn. One model can learn everything, if it is big enough and shaped for it. Each benchmark asks for something different: farming only needs the character just before, and so does forecasting an average field; recall has to find a pair far back; reversal needs to know where each waymark was; induction has to look back for what followed the same letter last time; sorting has to find the word in a name that settles its kind. Checkpoints Crafting A Checkpoint holds one model: its machines, its weights, how long it trained and its scores. Saving runs every test first, so the scores on a checkpoint are always the ones it earned. Saving over a checkpoint replaces the model on it. How big a model may be An agent can carry a model of up to 40,000 parameters in its head. A bigger model stays in a Model Server and is asked over relays: see Serving Models. The Train tab counts a model's parameters. Reading ahead A model that can see the letter it is asked to predict is not predicting anything. The Core checks every model for this. A model that reads ahead scores very well and means nothing; its checkpoint says so, and the Reader turns it away.

title: Ruins
text: Ruins The old world left three kinds of building behind. They stand in grassland, forest, taiga, snow, savanna, desert, hills, cherry groves and badlands, far apart: it takes travel to find them. Archive houses Small houses of calcite and tuff, one corner usually fallen in. They kept the archive. Look in the chest and the barrels, and brush the suspicious gravel where the corner came down. Relay masts Tall copper masts with an old relay still on top and a chest at the foot. The old world talked across distances with them; their chests hold relay cards and the plans for relays. Buried vaults A lantern on a post beside a trapdoor in the ground. Below is a deep room with a bank of old accelerators, and two chests. Every vault holds a salvaged model and photomasks for the most advanced machines. What they hold Archive Shard: pieces of the archive. See The Archive. Photomasks with salvaged designs: the Fabricator makes working but unfused machines from them, without a Bench. Linear layer, softmax and GELU masks turn up in houses, matrix multiply ones under the gravel, and attention, layer norm, feed-forward and transformer masks in vaults. See The Bench and the Fabricator. Schematic: Relays: the plans for relays, a pattern to copy that stays in the crafting grid. On masts and in vaults. Weight Crystal, blank Checkpoints and a little gold. Salvaged Model: see Salvaged Models.

title: Salvaged Models
text: Salvaged Models Every buried vault holds a Salvaged Model: the record of a model the old world built and could not make work. It keeps the model's machines, what it practised on and how it was trained. Each failed the way models often do. Rebuilding Put a salvaged model in a Model Core's Data slot and press Rebuild on the Data tab. Its machines are built in front of the Core as they were found: they need clear space, and they drop nothing when broken. Its training settings come with it. Train it as it is first, and watch how it fails. The loss curve, the Inspect tab and the machines themselves all have something to say. Repairing Find what is wrong and put it right: change a machine's settings, add or replace a machine, or change how it trains. A salvaged model has a budget of 1,500 steps per run to reach its goal; when a run runs out, Reset its weights and try again. A repaired model is worth experience, and what it took to repair it is worth more.

title: Shapes
text: Shapes Every value in a model is a grid of numbers, a tensor, and its shape says how big each side of the grid is. The Model Core checks every shape before it trains anything, the same way PyTorch would fail on the first batch, but with a clearer message. Reading a shape Shapes are written outermost first: [B×T×32] is a batch of B sequences, each T positions long, with 32 numbers at every position. Letter Means B Batch: how many sequences are processed at once. Set on the Core. T Time: positions in a sequence, up to the context length of 64. Every other number is a size you chose, like the 32 above, or the vocabulary size V, which shows as its value: 78, one for each letter, digit and mark a model knows, and the line break, or more with a tokenizer. The last dimension is the one machines work on: a Linear Layer turns [B×T×32] into [B×T×64] by mixing the 32 numbers at each position into 64 new ones, the same way at every position. A shape with fewer dimensions stretches to fit, as in PyTorch: the Position Table's [T×32] adds onto every sequence of a [B×T×32] batch. What the Core expects The Core sends out token ids, shaped [B×T], and wants back one score for every possible next token at every position: [B×T×V]. Whatever happens in between is up to you. When shapes disagree Press Check on the Core, or look at a machine. A machine whose inputs don't fit says what it got and what it needs. Common causes: A Residual Junction or Gate whose two inputs have different widths. A Matrix Multiplier whose inner sizes don't match. With Transpose on, it multiplies by the side input turned on its side, which is what comparing queries with keys needs. The last machine before the Core not ending in V. Shapes flow forward, so fix the earliest problem first: a wrong width early on makes every later machine look wrong too. The Inspect tab on the Core lists every machine in the order data reaches it. In PyTorch Shape errors are the most common bug in real model code. PyTorch only finds them when the code runs; reading shapes the way the Core does, before running anything, is a habit worth taking with you.

title: The Residual Stream
text: The Residual Stream A transformer is built around a running sum. The embedding starts it; every layer reads it, computes something, and adds its result back; the last layer turns the sum into scores. That running sum is the residual stream. A Residual Stream is a conduit for it. Crafting How it flows Each block passes the stream on out of its front. The chevrons on its sides point the way. An output touching a stream block, face to face or through a cable, adds into the stream at that block. An input touching a stream block reads the stream as it arrives there, before that block's additions. An input at the front of the last block reads the whole sum. A stream starts out empty: the first thing added to it, usually the embedding, is what it carries from there on. A stream placed against the front of another one carries on from it, and one placed against an output starts there. Sneak-use a face to turn a block. A layer on the stream This is one transformer layer, laid out the way it is usually drawn: read, normalize, compute, add back. Stack more layers by making the stream longer. The Transformer Block does all of this inside one block, residual additions included, so it goes on a line of its own, not on a stream: there it would add the stream to itself twice. Why a stream Each layer refines the sum rather than replacing it, so a layer that has nothing useful to add yet can leave it alone. Training sees the same shortcut: the gradient flows back along the stream to every layer directly. In a plain stack of layers it has to pass through every layer on the way down, and in a deep one it fades before it reaches the bottom. You can watch it happen: the amber wave that runs back while a model trains reaches every layer on a stream as bright as it started, and dims layer by layer down a deep plain stack. Rules Two streams can't flow into one block, and a stream can't run in a circle. A machine reads the stream where its input touches it and adds where its output does. Reading after the place it adds back would make a loop. A cable touching a stream and nothing else that drives it carries the stream. A cable touching two streams and no output carries neither: hold a Tensor Probe to see what a cable carries.

title: Tokens
text: Tokens A model never sees text, only tokens: numbers that each stand for a piece of text. Without a tokenizer, every character is a token, 78 in all: the letters, digits and marks, the space and the line break. Reading by the character is simple but short-sighted. Every word costs several predictions, and the 64 tokens a model reads at once cover only 64 characters. The BPE Forge The BPE Forge learns a vocabulary from the text on an Archive Drive by byte-pair encoding: Start with the characters. Count every pair of neighbouring tokens in the text. Join the most frequent pair into one new token, everywhere it occurs. Repeat until the vocabulary is as big as you asked. So t and h become th, th and e become the, and a space and the become ␣the. Common words end up as single tokens and rare ones stay in pieces, so any text can still be written. Merges stay inside a word: a word keeps the space before it, every digit stands alone, and punctuation keeps to itself. Crafting Put in a drive and a Tokenizer, pick a size, and watch the drive's text fall into fewer, longer tokens. Every merge is written onto the tokenizer as soon as it is learned, so you can take it out at any time. The forge carries on from the merges a tokenizer already has. A bigger size keeps every token of a smaller one, and a smaller size cuts a tokenizer back to the vocabulary it was on its way through. Crafting (Shapeless) Using a tokenizer Put the tokenizer in the Model Core's Tokenizer slot, and models built there read and write its tokens. Archive text in the data slots is cut into them, and so is whatever you say to the model through a Terminal. Datasets and the orders agents are given are always spelled out one character at a time, which every vocabulary can do. The tokenizer sets V: the rows of the embedding's table and the scores the last layer gives. Changing it reshapes those layers, so they start over. A saved model keeps the tokenizer it was trained with. What size? Longer tokens see further. At 512 tokens, a token of archive text carries about two and a half characters, so 64 tokens reach back about 160 characters instead of 64. More tokens cost weights. The embedding has a row and the last layer a score for every token: V × width weights each. Rare tokens learn slowly. A token seen only a few times in practice has little to learn from. Losses are counted per character, not per token, so models with different tokenizers compare fairly: a token's loss is shared among the characters it stands for.

title: Training
text: Training Training repeats one step thousands of times: run the model on a batch of text, measure how wrong it was, work out which way every weight should move to be less wrong, and move them a little. The loss A language model scores every possible next token. Softmax turns those scores into probabilities: The loss is the cross-entropy: the average, over every position, of how surprised the model was by the token that actually came next. A model that knows nothing spreads its bets evenly over all V tokens, and so starts near Every curve starts there. A loss of 0 would mean certainty about every next token, which no honest model reaches on real text. Losses are counted per character: a token's loss is shared among the characters it stands for, so a model that reads with a tokenizer compares fairly with one that reads by the character. For datasets, where only some positions have a right answer, the Core also measures accuracy: how often the top-scoring token is the right one. Practice and test The training loss is measured on the batches the model practises on, averaged over recent steps. The test loss is measured on examples practice never shows. When the two part ways, with training loss still falling while the test loss stalls or rises, the model is memorising its practice instead of learning what generalises. Models are judged on their tests alone. The settings Learning rate (LR). How far each step moves the weights. Too small and nothing happens for a long time; too large and the loss jumps around or explodes. The Core trains with AdamW, the optimizer most language models use. It scales each weight's step by the size of its recent gradients, so the learning rate sets the step size fairly directly: with the usual β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999 and weight decay λ = 0.01 on weight matrices. The first 20 steps warm up from zero to the full learning rate. Batch. How many sequences each step looks at. Bigger batches give a steadier gradient but cost more per step. Clip. Gradient clipping caps the size of the whole gradient before the step: It rescues the occasional huge gradient without changing ordinary steps. It does not rescue a learning rate that is too large on every step. Speed. Watch trains slowly enough to follow the curve; Max trains as fast as the Core can. Reading the curve Flat at the start, then a sudden drop: the model found a mechanism. Attention models often do this. Falling, then flattening above the goal: the model has learned all it can see. Give it more to work with: more context, more width, more layers. Jagged and climbing: the steps are too big. Lower the learning rate. Both losses suspiciously low: something lets the model see the answer. The Core flags a model that reads ahead. Watching it learn While a model trains, waves run through its blocks every two seconds. A teal pulse travels from the tokens to the loss, lighting each machine as the batch reaches it, as brightly as the values it puts out. Then an amber pulse runs back from the loss, lighting each machine as brightly as the gradient that reaches it. A machine that stays dark on the way back hardly learns: almost no gradient reaches it. Above each machine floats its output for one example of practice: a bar per entry for a vector, a cell per entry for a matrix, amber above zero and blue below. An attention head shows its pattern instead, which earlier tokens each token looks at. Look at a hologram to read the value under your crosshair. Hold a Tensor Probe to see the holograms when nothing is training. When training stops Training stops when you press Stop or when a machine of the model changes. It also stops when the loss diverges: if it turns into NaN, or climbs far above where it started. A salvaged model adds a budget: a limited number of steps per run, after which you reset the weights and try again. Reset throws the learned weights away so the next run starts fresh. Check reads the model again and reports any problem without training.

title: Machines and Cables
text: Machines and Cables A model is a graph of operations, and you build that graph out of blocks. Values flow out of one machine and into the next through cables, from the Model Core's tokens to the scores it takes back. Ports Every machine computes one output from its inputs, and each face of the block has a job: Front: the output. Back: the main input. Every other face: the side input, on machines that take two inputs, such as the Residual Junction or the Matrix Multiplier. One-input machines leave their sides unused, and the Position Table has no input at all. The Model Core sends tokens out of its front and takes the finished scores in through any other face. Look at a machine to see which port the face under your crosshair is. A machine placed against another machine's output takes that output as its input; placed against an input, it feeds it; placed against a cable or a residual stream, it reads it. Anywhere else its output points away from you. Sneak-use a face to turn the output to that face; sneak-using the output face itself turns the machine around. Networks Cables that touch form a network, and a network carries exactly one value. So every network needs exactly one source, a machine's front or the Core's front, and any number of inputs may read it. Two sources on one network is an error, and so is an input on a network with no source. Colors Colored cables only join cables of their own color, while plain cables join any color. That lets two networks run side by side without mixing. Dye eight cables at a time; a water bucket washes the color out again. Crafting Crafting Tracing a value With a Tensor Probe in hand, looking at a cable tells you which machine drives it and how many inputs read it. Use the probe on a cable to list every port on its network in chat. The probe also shows every machine's output as a hologram above it, from the last time the model ran: look at one to read its values. See Training for what they show while a model learns.
